{{Short description|Coherent risk measure using weighted outcomes based on risk aversion}}
A '''Spectral risk measure''' is a [[risk measure]] given as a [[weighted average]] of outcomes where bad outcomes are, typically, included with larger weights. A spectral risk measure is a function of [[portfolio (finance)|portfolio]] returns and outputs the amount of the [[numeraire]] (typically a [[currency]]) to be kept in reserve.  A spectral risk measure is always a [[coherent risk measure]], but the converse does not always hold.  An advantage of spectral measures is the way in which they can be related to [[risk aversion]], and particularly to a [[utility function]], through the weights given to the possible portfolio returns.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Extreme spectral risk measures: An application to futures clearinghouse margin requirements|first1=John|last1=Cotter|first2=Kevin|last2=Dowd|journal=Journal of Banking & Finance|volume=30|issue=12|date=December 2006|pages=3469–3485|doi=10.1016/j.jbankfin.2006.01.008|arxiv=1103.5653}}</ref>

== Definition ==

Consider a [[portfolio (finance)|portfolio]] <math>X</math> (denoting the portfolio payoff).  Then a spectral risk measure <math>M_{\phi}: \mathcal{L} \to \mathbb{R}</math> where <math>\phi</math> is non-negative, non-increasing, [[Continuous function#Directional and semi-continuity|right-continuous]], integrable function defined on <math>[0,1]</math> such that <math>\int_0^1 \phi(p)dp = 1</math> is defined by
:<math>M_{\phi}(X) = -\int_0^1 \phi(p) F_X^{-1}(p) dp</math>
where <math>F_X</math> is the [[cumulative distribution function]] for ''X''.<ref name="Adam" /><ref>{{cite journal|title=Spectral Risk Measures: Properties and Limitations|first1=Kevin|last1=Dowd|first2=John|last2=Cotter|first3=Ghulam|last3=Sorwar|year=2008|journal=CRIS Discussion Paper Series|issue=2|url=http://www.nottingham.ac.uk/business/cris/papers/2008-2.pdf|accessdate=October 13, 2011}}</ref>

If there are <math>S</math> equiprobable outcomes with the corresponding payoffs given by the [[order statistics]] <math>X_{1:S}, ... X_{S:S}</math>. Let <math>\phi\in\mathbb{R}^S</math>. The measure
<math>M_{\phi}:\mathbb{R}^S\rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> defined by <math>M_{\phi}(X)=-\delta\sum_{s=1}^S\phi_sX_{s:S}</math> is a '''spectral measure of risk''' if <math>\phi\in\mathbb{R}^S</math> satisfies the conditions

# Nonnegativity: <math>\phi_s\geq0 </math> for all <math>s=1, \dots, S</math>,
# Normalization: <math>\sum_{s=1}^S\phi_s=1</math>,
# Monotonicity : <math>\phi_s</math> is non-increasing, that is <math>\phi_{s_1}\geq\phi_{s_2}</math> if <math>{s_1}<{s_2}</math> and <math>{s_1}, {s_2}\in\{1,\dots,S\}</math>.<ref>{{Citation
 | last=Acerbi
 | first=Carlo
 | author-link=
 | publication-date=2002
 | year=2002
 | title=Spectral measures of risk: A coherent representation of subjective risk aversion
 | periodical=[[Journal of Banking and Finance]]
 | location=

 | volume=26

==Properties==
Spectral risk measures are also [[Coherent risk measure|coherent]].  Every spectral risk measure <math>\rho: \mathcal{L} \to \mathbb{R}</math> satisfies:
# Positive Homogeneity: for every portfolio ''X'' and positive value <math>\lambda > 0</math>, <math>\rho(\lambda X) = \lambda \rho(X)</math>;
# Translation-Invariance: for every portfolio ''X'' and <math>\alpha \in \mathbb{R}</math>, <math>\rho(X + a) = \rho(X) - a</math>;
# Monotonicity: for all portfolios ''X'' and ''Y'' such that <math>X \geq Y</math>, <math>\rho(X) \leq \rho(Y)</math>;
# Sub-additivity: for all portfolios ''X'' and ''Y'', <math>\rho(X+Y) \leq \rho(X) + \rho(Y)</math>; 
# Law-Invariance: for all portfolios ''X'' and ''Y'' with [[cumulative distribution function]]s <math>F_X</math> and <math>F_Y</math> respectively, if <math>F_X = F_Y</math> then <math>\rho(X) = \rho(Y)</math>;
# Comonotonic Additivity: for every [[comonotonicity|comonotonic]] random variables ''X'' and ''Y'', <math>\rho(X+Y) = \rho(X) + \rho(Y)</math>.  Note that ''X'' and ''Y'' are comonotonic if for every <math>\omega_1,\omega_2 \in \Omega: \; (X(\omega_2) - X(\omega_1))(Y(\omega_2) - Y(\omega_1)) \geq 0</math>.<ref name="Adam">{{cite journal|title=Spectral risk measures and portfolio selection|year=2007|first1=Alexandre|last1=Adam|first2=Mohamed|last2=Houkari|first3=Jean-Paul|last3=Laurent|url=http://laurent.jeanpaul.free.fr/Spectral_risk_measures_and_portfolio_selection.pdf|accessdate=October 11, 2011}}</ref>
In some texts{{which|date=October 2016}} the input ''X'' is interpreted as losses rather than payoff of a portfolio.  In this case, the translation-invariance property would be given by <math>\rho(X+a) = \rho(X) + a</math>, and the monotonicity property by <math>X \geq Y \implies \rho(X) \geq \rho(Y)</math> instead of the above.

== Examples ==
* The [[expected shortfall]] is a spectral measure of risk.
* The [[expected value]] is ''trivially'' a spectral measure of risk.
